title: Workshop 1 — Introducing AI for DH Pedagogy

image.alt: HAL 9000 — the on-screen AI we've been arguing with for fifty years

slides.title: ELIZA and the ELIZA effect
slides.lead: Before we touch a tool, we look back. The conversation we're having about AI in 2026 has a 60-year-old prologue — and the prologue has the answers.

slides.title: ELIZA, 1966
bullets: Joseph **Weizenbaum** at MIT, 1964–66.
About 200 lines of code. Pattern-matches your sentence and reflects it back.
Best-known script: **DOCTOR** — a parody of Rogerian ("person-centered") therapy.
Try [the modern web ELIZA](https://www.masswerk.at/eliza/) for ten minutes. Notice where it breaks.

image.alt: Screenshot of a modern web ELIZA conversation

quote: I was startled to see how quickly and how very deeply people conversing with DOCTOR became emotionally involved with the computer and how unequivocally they anthropomorphized it.

Once my secretary, who had watched me work on the program for many months and therefore surely knew it to be merely a computer program, started conversing with it. After only a few interchanges with it, she asked me to leave the room.
slides.attribution: Joseph Weizenbaum, *Computer Power and Human Reason* (1976) — the **ELIZA effect** named

slides.title: The two roads from 1966
bullets: **Weizenbaum**: spent the rest of his life as a critic of AI hype. His worry wasn't that ELIZA was *too smart* — it was that humans were too willing to believe it was.
**Marvin Minsky** (across the hall): founded the MIT AI Laboratory, took Pentagon funding unhindered, championed the dream.
Both roads are still open in 2026. We are walking them at the same time.

image.alt: Portrait/contextual image about Weizenbaum and ELIZA

slides.quote: We are trying to do the same thing Weizenbaum tried to do: educate people about how these systems work, dispel the notion that they are thinking machines with a semblance of human understanding, and provide a model of how to think about them instead.
slides.attribution: Emily Bender & Alex Hanna, *The AI Con* (2025) — explicitly picking up Weizenbaum's thread

slides.title: Try ELIZA
slides.prompt: Five minutes — open it up and notice what your brain does:
steps: Type as if you're talking to a therapist. Use whatever's actually on your mind.
Notice the pattern: ELIZA reflects your nouns, asks open questions, occasionally trips.
Catch yourself anthropomorphising. **That's the ELIZA effect.** It's still the strongest force in the room when we use ChatGPT.

slides.title: AI, LLMs, and how they work
slides.lead: What an LLM actually is — in plain language. Then what sits on top of it: reasoning layers, RLHF, and the choices that turn a base model into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini.

slides.title: What is generative AI?
bullets: Per the **MLA-CCCC task force**: 'computer systems that can produce, or generate, various forms of traditionally human expression — language, images, video, music.'
Today we're focused on the *language* part. We touch the others in later workshops.
Transformer architecture + a vast scraped training corpus + reasoning layers on top.
[MLA-CCCC working paper →](https://aiandwriting.hcommons.org/working-paper-1/)

image.alt: Definitional slide: What is generative AI?

slides.quote: "AI" is a marketing term. It doesn't refer to a coherent set of technologies. Instead, the phrase is deployed when the people building or selling a particular set of technologies will profit from getting others to believe that their technology is similar to humans.
slides.attribution: Emily Bender & Alex Hanna, *The AI Con*

slides.title: AI is a field. Deep learning is one method. LLMs are one application.
bullets: **AI** — the broad goal of machines that act intelligently.
**Machine learning** — the subfield where systems learn patterns from data.
**Deep learning** — one ML approach using many-layered neural networks.
**LLMs** — a particular use of deep-learning transformers, trained to predict tokens.
When the news says "AI did X," almost always: an LLM did X.

slides.title: Language model, plain version
bullets: A language model assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens.
*Large* language models do this with billions of parameters.
**Pretraining** is the long, expensive step (weeks or months on GPU clusters).
**Inference** is what happens when you type a prompt.
Everything else — RLHF, system prompts, tools — sits **on top** of the pretrained model.

quote: An LLM is a machine learning model that can complete a sentence of text. Give the model the phrase "the cat sat on the " and it will (almost certainly) suggest "mat" as the next word in the sentence.
As these models get larger and train on increasing amounts of data, they can complete more complex sentences — like "a python function to download a file from a URL is `def download_file(url):` ".

LLMs don't actually work directly with words — they work with **tokens**. A sequence of text is converted into a sequence of integer tokens, so "the cat sat on the " becomes `[3086, 9059, 10139, 402, 290, 220]`. This is worth understanding because LLM providers charge based on the number of tokens processed, and are limited in how many tokens they can consider at a time.

slides.title: Try tokenizing a sentence
slides.prompt: Two minutes — take Willison's point off the page:
steps: Open the [OpenAI Tokenizer](https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer) in a new tab.
Paste a sentence you'd actually type into Claude or ChatGPT.
Note the **token count** and which 'words' the tokenizer splits into multiple pieces.
Try the same sentence in another language, with a typo, or stuffed with your discipline's jargon. Watch what changes.

slides.title: What sits on top of the base model
bullets: **RLHF** (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): humans rank model outputs; the model learns to prefer the ranked-good ones.
**System prompts**: invisible instructions that set tone, role, refusals.
**Tools**: web search, code execution, file access — the model decides when to call them.
The Opus / Sonnet / Haiku family is **the same family of base models** at different sizes — your choice trades depth for speed and cost.

slides.title: The ChatGPT moment
slides.lead: November 30, 2022. The technology wasn't new. The interface was. And the interface was the event.

slides.title: Before ChatGPT, programmers already had this
bullets: **[June 11, 2020](https://techcrunch.com/2020/06/11/openai-makes-an-all-purpose-api-for-its-text-based-ai-capabilities/):** OpenAI releases the GPT-3 API in private beta. Developers could already prompt the model behind a waiting list.

**[June 29, 2021](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/introducing-github-copilot-ai-pair-programmer/):** GitHub Copilot enters technical preview — built on OpenAI Codex, an OpenAI model descended from GPT-3.
**[November 18, 2021](https://venturebeat.com/ai/openai-makes-gpt-3-generally-available-through-its-api/):** the GPT-3 API drops the waitlist; it's now open to any developer.
Faculty and students mostly didn't know any of this was happening.

slides.title: November 30, 2022
bullets: OpenAI launches **[ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/)** — a free web demo of a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 ([announcement post](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/)).
**[1 million users in 5 days](https://x.com/sama/status/1599668808285028353).** (Sam Altman's announcement tweet, Dec 5, 2022.)

**[~100 million monthly active users by January 2023](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/)** — UBS analysts: "In 20 years following the internet space, we cannot recall a faster ramp in a consumer internet app."
The *model* had been around for over two years. The *chat box* was the news.
slides.caption: Sources: [Sam Altman on X](https://x.com/sama/status/1599668808285028353), [Reuters / UBS analyst note](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/).

quote: The chatbot was the wrapping. The model was already there.

What changed on November 30, 2022 wasn't a leap in capability — it was a leap in **access**. Anyone with a browser and an email address could talk to a system that had previously lived behind an API key, a credit card, and a developer account.
Every higher-ed conversation about generative AI is a conversation about that access. The crisis isn't that the model exists. It's that the model became *visible to everyone at once*.
slides.attribution: Workshop framing — what the ChatGPT moment was actually about

slides.title: Where this leaves us — and where it's going
slides.lead: The chatbot was the wrapping. Now the wrapping is shifting again — toward agents that *use* the LLM as a substrate, not as a product.

slides.title: From plagiarism panic to agent panic
bullets: Plagiarism panics, AI-detector arms race, faculty caught between adoption pressure and pedagogical challenges.
*"A new app offers to do students' work for them. Professors aren't ready."*
The conversation has shifted from *did the chatbot write this?* to *did the agent do the work?*

image.alt: Chronicle of Higher Education article header: Will Agentic AI Break Higher Education?

slides.caption: [*The Chronicle of Higher Education* — "Will Agentic AI Break Higher Education?"](https://www.chronicle.com/article/will-agentic-ai-break-higher-education)

slides.title: What is an agent?
bullets: **Tool use:** the model can call functions you give it (web search, file edit, run command).
**Planning:** the model decides what to do next, in what order, and when to stop.
**Subagents:** the model can spawn helper instances of itself for sub-tasks.
An *agent* is the loop these compose into. The vocabulary is doing a lot of work — but the foundation is still the LLM we just described.

slides.title: The LLM is now the substrate, not the product
bullets: **2022:** the chatbot *is* the product (ChatGPT).
**2026:** the chatbot is one interface among many. Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, MCP-connected research tools, agent platforms.
Same family of models underneath. Different *wrappers* — and the wrapping is where pedagogical choices live now.
Everything else in this series — Projects, Artifacts, Code Web, CLI — is a wrapper choice.

slides.title: Build our own ELIZA — together, in Claude Artifacts
slides.prompt: We close where we opened. Same idea, sixty years later, with room for our own voice:
steps: Open [Claude](https://claude.ai/) and start a new chat.

Prompt together: *"Build a Claude Artifact: a chatbot **in the spirit of** Weizenbaum's 1966 ELIZA — pattern-match the user's input and reflect it back as questions. Style and tone are yours: a snarky librarian, a doom-prophet, a noir detective, a Rogerian therapist. Don't pretend to know more than the pattern."*
Open the Artifact in the side panel. Talk to it the way you talked to ELIZA earlier.
**Compare.** What does Claude do that pattern-matching can't? What does it do that pattern-matching *also* did? Where does the ELIZA effect kick in this time?
Save the Artifact URL — bring the comparison to next week's discussion.

slides.title: Three things to leave with
slides.lead: After today you should be able to explain to a colleague: where ELIZA started this, what an LLM actually is and what sits on top of it, why the ChatGPT *interface* was the event, and what "agentic" adds to the conversation.
